projectsPage.lede: Laid out along a timeline, from the first project to now. Each stop has a page of its own: the context, the decisions made, and screenshots from the running build.

chanh-toa.tagline: A parish portal: mass times across 27 dioceses, the full Bible, and answers on faith.
chanh-toa.summary: Mass times change constantly and nobody announces it. Travel a little, want to attend, and you end up asking around. This site exists so that question has one place to be answered.
chanh-toa.techNote: Next.js with React and TypeScript, the interface in Tailwind, the server side on Node.js, data in Firebase and Firestore, images processed with Sharp. Posts arrive from the parish Facebook page through the Graph API. Server rendering was the choice because most of this site is material search engines need to read: Mass times, every chapter of Scripture, every question of faith.

highlights.title: The question people ask most
highlights.body: Turn on location and you see the nearest church and how long until the next Mass, across data covering 27 dioceses. Because the schedule keeps shifting, parishioners can correct it right on the card — the information stays alive through its readers, not through a one-time import.

highlights.title: Then come the questions people hesitate to ask
highlights.body: After Mass times come the things people are shy to raise in person: the sacraments, moral questions, marriage. Each has a short answer to skim, and a longer one with catechism sources for anyone who wants to follow it through.

highlights.title: The whole of Scripture, chapter by chapter
highlights.body: Old and New Testament in full, an illustration for each book, and an address of its own for every chapter so it can be sent straight to someone. The prayer section counts readings and keeps a daily streak — better at holding a habit than any reminder.

highlights.title: Wired straight into the parish page
highlights.body: The parish already posts to its own Facebook page, and nobody wants to post a second time. The server calls the Facebook Graph API on a schedule, pulls new posts and their images, compresses them with Sharp and stores them in Firestore — post once on the page and it appears in both places. The access key stays on the server, guarded by Firestore rules, and never travels down to the browser; every write must carry an administrator identity.

shots.kinh-nguyen: Core prayers, with a counter and a daily streak.
shots.gioi-thieu: About — the parish history told in four chapters.

chanh-toa.closing: The site is live and parishioners open it daily. For a parish portal, success isn't traffic — it's that nobody has to phone around to find out when Mass is.

hwj.tagline: A luxury jewellery e-commerce system on MERN: metal-linked pricing, server-verified PayPal checkout, one admin dashboard.
hwj.summary: Coursework for COMP1842 Web Programming 2, University of Greenwich (Vietnam): digitising the whole jewellery business, from product presentation to financial transactions and after-sales management.
hwj.techNote: A MERN architecture in four layers: a React 19 + TypeScript interface (Vite, Zustand, Tailwind, Material UI); a Node.js/Express REST server; MongoDB Atlas through Mongoose; and third-party services — Google OAuth 2.0, the PayPal SDK and Cloudinary.

highlights.title: Payments verified on the server
highlights.body: After PayPal reports success, the backend calls the PayPal API to reconcile status and amount. An order whose total differs from PayPal's figure is rejected, so a payment result cannot be forged from the browser.

highlights.title: Layered security
highlights.body: Customers sign in with Google OAuth 2.0 and sessions are held by JWT. Admin passwords are hashed with bcrypt; admin APIs sit behind role checks, an API key, CORS and rate limiting.

highlights.title: A flexible data model for jewellery
highlights.body: MongoDB stores each piece's variable attributes (karat, metal weight, stones, SKU) as documents. Mongoose enforces required fields and unique voucher and product codes; hooks update total spend and loyalty points after every order.

highlights.title: One dashboard for all operations
highlights.body: When an admin signs in, the account page becomes a dashboard: products (images on Cloudinary), orders, consultation appointments, support tickets, customers and system settings such as vouchers and shipping fees.

hwj.closing: The biggest lesson: most of a full-stack project's success lies in getting the data structure right from the start, and the defences that matter most always belong on the backend.

report.title: Project report
report.abstract: HWJ (Hugo Wishpax Jewellery) is a luxury jewellery e-commerce system built on a full-stack MERN architecture. The project aims to digitise the jewellery business, from product presentation to financial transactions and after-sales management. Its core differentiator is the integration of a real service chain: precious-metal prices that follow the market, third-party authentication, payments reconciled on the server and transparent electronic invoices. The system implements full CRUD with a clear separation of permissions between customers and administrators.

sections.title: Development process
paragraphs: The project followed an iterative and incremental model, allowing quality control after each cycle and flexible integration of new features. It ran in six phases:
list: Business requirements: defining customer and admin roles, the order flow, and warranty and return policies specific to jewellery.
Overall architecture: separating the interface (React), server (Express/Node.js), database (MongoDB) and third-party integration layer (PayPal, Cloudinary).
Interface and navigation design: a standard sitemap for both customers and administrators.
Data model design: normalised entities, validation and query indexes.
Security and payments: JWT authentication, protected admin APIs, rate limiting and server-side PayPal verification.
Integration testing: manual end-to-end testing of every business flow.

sections.title: Interface and navigation design
paragraphs: The interface follows a Luxury Minimalism style with the brand colours #ec003f and #020618. Pages are grouped by task to shape the customer journey: Explore (Heritage, Collections, Product Detail), Transaction (Cart, Confirm Order, Valuation), Service (Appointment, Policies, Support) and Account (member profile and admin dashboard).

Client-side navigation is handled by React Router; the server is split into independent REST modules behind the /api gateway: /auth and /admins for identity, /products, /orders and /vouchers for the core business, /appointments and /support/tickets for customer care, and /settings for system configuration.

subsections.title: Front end
subsections.body: A single-page application in React 19 and TypeScript; TypeScript types for Product and Order catch errors during development in the complex checkout flow. Zustand manages global state (cart, session, settings) without prop drilling. Tailwind CSS handles layout and Material UI provides data tables and forms (React, 2024; Zustand, 2024).

subsections.title: Back end
subsections.body: Node.js and Express provide a REST API split into modules (Auth, Products, Orders, Appointments), so features such as vouchers can be added without touching the rest. JWT holds sessions; bcrypt hashes admin passwords; middleware applies CORS, brute-force rate limiting and an admin-only API key check. The key technical point is verifying the final payment status through the PayPal API on the server (Node.js Foundation, 2024; PayPal Developer, 2024).

subsections.title: Database
subsections.body: MongoDB Atlas stores documents, which suits jewellery's variable attributes without the migrations of a traditional SQL schema. Mongoose enforces required fields, email format and unique voucher and product codes; hooks recalculate loyalty points and total spend after each successful order; order numbers and customer emails are indexed (MongoDB, 2024).

subsections.title: Rationale
subsections.body: One language, JavaScript, across interface and server allows shared logic such as validation and reduces context switching. MongoDB's NoSQL model and Node.js's asynchronous processing let the system scale when traffic peaks during promotions.

subsections.title: GDPR compliance
subsections.body: The system follows Privacy by Design: it collects only what a transaction needs (email, phone, address) and states the purpose in the Privacy Policy, in line with data minimisation under Article 5 GDPR. Customers can view and edit their data and ask for consultation history to be deleted. Full compliance would add machine-readable data export and records of processing activities (European Parliament and Council, 2016).

subsections.title: Ethical design
subsections.body: The interface avoids dark patterns: cancelling an appointment or clearing the cart is easy, respecting customer autonomy. Loyalty points and vouchers are computed on the backend for fairness. Server-side payment verification is both a technical measure and a commitment to protecting customers' money (Gotterbarn, Miller and Rogerson, 1997; OWASP Foundation, 2021).

sections.title: Testing and evaluation
paragraphs: Testing combined two methods: static checks with ESLint and TypeScript type checking on the front end, and manual business-flow testing that simulated users from product search and payment through to after-sales service.

sections.title: Limitations and future work
list: Test automation: move from manual testing to unit, integration and end-to-end tests with Jest or Cypress.
SEO and performance: move to Next.js for server-side rendering so products are easier for search engines to index.
AI: a consultation chatbot based on customer preferences and automatic categorisation of support tickets.
Interface: further optimisation for mobile devices and users of all ages.

sections.title: Reflection
paragraphs: Technically, the project showed how to join the separate parts of MERN into one system, from a flexible MongoDB schema to an optimised React 19 interface; managing state with Zustand changed how I approach SPA performance.

The hardest part was integrating the PayPal SDK and verifying payments on the server for financial accuracy, alongside syncing the cart, handling API errors and balancing aesthetics with load speed when serving high-quality images through Cloudinary.
The biggest lesson was to design the data structure correctly from the start, and that the important defences belong on the backend rather than the client.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: HWJ meets its goal of a specialised e-commerce platform for luxury jewellery. The MERN architecture addresses three demands: a refined experience, flexible data management and secure financial transactions. The project brings together full-stack programming, UI/UX design standards and real business processes.

minh-oi-media.tagline: A wedding documentary studio site — pricing, portfolio and the enquiry flow.
minh-oi-media.summary: Couples choose a wedding studio with three tabs open at once. The one that makes them message first to learn the price gets closed first. Every decision here comes out of that one observation.
minh-oi-media.techNote: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no framework at all. A page presenting five service packages does not need React; without a framework it stays light, opens fast on mobile data, and the client can edit the words in the file without calling anyone.

highlights.title: People ask the price before the name
highlights.body: The wedding trade likes to hide prices to force an enquiry. Here the five packages sit right on the path, each listing exactly what the couple receives — readers rule themselves out, or in, before anyone has to answer a message.

highlights.title: The photograph speaks first
highlights.body: The first screen is a full-bleed wedding photograph, not a slogan. For a studio, that first image is the entire proof of competence; every line of copy after it is only there to explain.

highlights.title: Portrait is the default
highlights.body: Almost everyone reads this on a phone, mid-conversation about which studio to book. So the price list folds into a single column, with no wide table to drag sideways.

highlights.title: And no framework was needed
highlights.body: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A page presenting five packages doesn't need React; without a framework it stays light, opens fast on 4G, and the studio can edit the words in the file without calling anyone.

shots.home: Home — a large photograph leads, the brand sits over it.
shots.bang-gia: Five packages, each spelling out what the client receives.

minh-oi-media.closing: Worked directly with the client, from the first requirements conversation through to handover. What they kept afterwards is a site they can look after themselves.

l3go-coffee.tagline: A coffee shop site — drinks picked by how you feel. UI/UX, with Jason Phan.
l3go-coffee.summary: A three-storey café in Cần Thơ, with a spiral staircase and walls of coloured glass brick. People choose a café by where they will sit, not by the coffee — so the site has to show the room before anyone decides to go.
l3go-coffee.techNote: React and Tailwind. My part was the interface and the experience: the colour system, the typographic rhythm, the flow through the menu, and how the photographs of the space are cropped. Jason Phan handled the data layer and deployment.

highlights.title: The room is the product
highlights.body: The spiral staircase, the glass-brick wall and the lattice of night lights are held at full size rather than chopped into a gallery. A reader needs to feel where their seat would be before caring what is on the menu.

highlights.title: A long menu nobody reads to the end
highlights.body: Sixty-eight items, and nobody reads a coffee-tea-frappé table all the way down. So the filters follow the feeling someone arrives with: need to wake up, want to settle down, staying a while with friends. Choosing by mood is faster than choosing by category.

highlights.title: My part, and his
highlights.body: Made with Jason Phan. Mine was the UI/UX: the colour system, the typographic rhythm, the flow through the menu and how the room is cropped. Building the data and shipping it was his — the line was clear from the start, so nobody stepped on anyone.

shots.home: Home — "The right drink for the mood."
shots.thuc-don: The menu, filtered by mood instead of category.
shots.khong-gian: The space page — three storeys, spiral staircase.

l3go-coffee.closing: A short project, but the clearest lesson in it: the hard part of a menu isn't listing dishes, it's helping someone stop hesitating.

mhike.tagline: A hiking-trip manager built twice: native Android (Java) and cross-platform (React Native).
mhike.summary: Coursework for COMP1786 Mobile Application Design and Development, University of Greenwich (Vietnam). Marked 77% and named Best Student in the module, Summer 2026.
mhike.techNote: Two implementations on one Firebase data branch. The native Android app is written in Java on an Activity–Adapter–Model structure. The cross-platform app is written in React Native (Expo) and TypeScript, organised local-first around SQLite.

highlights.title: Local-first for a setting without signal
highlights.body: The React Native app writes every operation to SQLite first, then mirrors it to Firebase on a best-effort basis. The app keeps working when the connection drops, which is the normal case on a trail.

highlights.title: The hike–observation relationship is preserved
highlights.body: The SQLite schema separates hikes and observations and enables foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE. One hike holds many observations; deleting a hike removes its observations.

highlights.title: Multi-criteria search with parameterised queries
highlights.body: Basic search matches a name prefix; advanced search builds a WHERE clause from name, location, length range, date range and difficulty, without concatenating user input into SQL.

highlights.title: Features beyond the specification
highlights.body: GPS journey tracking, weather, an SOS beacon, a 12-week training plan, an English–Vietnamese interface and a dark theme.

mhike.closing: Building one app two ways made it clear that a finished-looking interface is not the same as meeting the specification.

report.title: Project report
report.abstract: This report evaluates two implementations of M-Hike: the MHike Android App, written natively in Java, and the cross-platform MHike App, written in React Native/Expo and TypeScript. The evaluation draws on the module specification, source-code review, experimental builds, runs on a Pixel 7 and an iPhone 16 Pro, and a logic test suite. The React Native implementation provides a more complete SQLite layer and advanced search, while the native implementation has a comparatively polished interface but departs from the specification in the role of SQLite, advanced search and the observation link during editing.

sections.title: Scope and method
list: Each requirement (a)–(g) of the brief was traced to the actual interface flow and source code.
The native app was built with Gradle, installed as a debug APK and run on a Pixel 7 emulator.
The React Native app was run on a Pixel 7 and an iPhone 16 Pro, with typecheck, lint, logic tests and an Expo web build to compare responsive layouts.
HCI, security, screen adaptability and deployment readiness were assessed against official documentation and OWASP MASVS.

sections.title: Architecture
paragraphs: The native Android app follows an Activity–Adapter–Model structure, uses Firebase Realtime Database as its primary store and SQLite as a cache for the hike list. This keeps the interface responsive but does not fully meet the requirement that SQLite be the storage mechanism for features (b) and (c).

The React Native app is local-first: db.ts manages SQLite (WAL mode, foreign keys) and api.ts wraps local operations and mirrors them to Firebase on a best-effort basis. This suits hiking, where connectivity is intermittent.

subsections.title: Human–computer interaction (HCI)
subsections.body: Large headings, cards on a neutral background, a five-item bottom bar, empty states and button-style choices reduce memory load. The form is grouped, pre-fills the date, supports GPS and confirms before saving. Native limitations: some required fields are blocked silently, the form is long in locked portrait, and TalkBack, large text and contrast are untested. Improvements: errors beside each field, focus moved to the first error, touch targets of at least 48 dp and 4.5:1 contrast (Android Developers, 2026a).

subsections.title: Security and privacy
subsections.body: Strengths: Google sign-in, internal Activities set to exported=false, offline caching in Firebase. Limitations: no Firebase Security Rules in the repository, the REST layer sends no ID token, encryptData is reversible Base64 encoding, and allowBackup is on. Priorities: Rules scoped to auth.uid, App Check, tokens in Keystore/SecureStore, minimal permissions and dependency scanning in CI (Firebase, 2026; OWASP Foundation, 2026).

subsections.title: Screen size and state
subsections.body: Both apps use dp/sp, ScrollView or Flexbox and work well on a phone in portrait. There is no layout for tablets, foldables or split screen. Improvements: window-size classes and useWindowDimensions for a list–detail layout, tested at 200% font size (Android Developers, 2026b; React Native, 2026).

subsections.title: Live deployment
subsections.body: A development/release build is needed instead of Expo Go, along with a single applicationId, a real Maps key, separate dev/staging/prod Firebase projects and a CI pipeline running Gradle, typecheck, lint, migration tests and App Bundle signing. Because the app handles location, photos and emergency contacts, a Data safety declaration and a privacy policy are required before release (Expo, 2026; Google Play, 2026).

sections.title: Reflection
paragraphs: The early phase prioritised the home screen, list, form and navigation, which produced a consistent experience early but left the foundational requirements — SQLite, the hike–observation relationship and advanced search — loosely traced. The most effective part was the local-first React Native prototype, where the schema, typecheck and logic tests caught errors without relying on manual runs.

Done again, a requirement–screen–data layer–test case matrix would come before any interface, each requirement would carry explicit acceptance criteria, and security would be part of the architecture from the start rather than handled at the end.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: M-Hike reaches a substantial functional base: hike CRUD, a multi-field form, observations, sign-in, GPS and several extensions, with the React Native app adding local-first SQLite and multi-criteria search. The next steps are moving native CRUD onto SQLite, completing native advanced search, configuring release builds, then locking down Firebase Rules, tokens and permissions before optimising for tablets.
